payload.title: The baseline exam reads the run vocabulary through two private literals, so crashed_tools lists only status 'crash' while tool_health.RUN_STATUSES has seven other non-ok outcomes (budget_exceeded, tool_unhealthy, integrity_failed and more); a run that ended that way is tallied as a finished tool with its findings, and the stamped tally carries no completeness field
evidence: tools/aria-acceptance/harness.py:737 (every run's status is stored, but only the count of findings reaches the tally)
tools/aria-acceptance/harness.py:846-849 (crashed_tools is status == 'crash' only; no other incompleteness is reported)
aria-kernel/aria_kernel/tool_health.py:38-52 (RUN_STATUSES: nine statuses, eight of them not ok)
payload.rule_violated: Every number carries what it was measured over (F1.3 stamping): a stamped tally must say which tools did not finish, using the kernel's one status vocabulary rather than a private literal.
payload.notes: A cycle in which one adapter timed out (budget_exceeded) or was refused as tool_unhealthy is read by the exam as a tool with zero or partial findings. crashed_tools stays empty, the console prints 'crashed: []', and the measurements.tally block, which is what --against compares and what the program stamps as the baseline, carries no marker that the number is a lower bound. Only the per-tool status in store.tools shows it. The kept store holds only ok and crash, so the exit run did not meet this; a re-baseline over a cycle with a timeout will. The evidence reviewer reproduced it on a store copy with one status edited to budget_exceeded. Close condition: Derive incomplete_tools from tool_health.RUN_STATUSES (every status other than ok) and compare the runner type with tool_registry.SUBPROCESS_RUNNER_TYPE; put incomplete_tools in the tally block, or refuse by name when any run is not ok. Add a test per non-ok status asserting the report names the tool and the tally flags itself as a lower bound. Verified at origin/main ae2958653d.
